title: JavaScript Fundamentals
description: Learn the core building blocks of JavaScript — the language that powers the modern web. Master variables, data types, operators, control flow, arrays, and objects with modern ES6+ syntax.
learningObjectives: Declare variables with let, const, and understand var's issues
Work with all JavaScript data types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, object, array
Use arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators
Write if/else, switch, and ternary expressions
Create and manipulate arrays and objects

sections.content: JavaScript has three ways to declare variables: var (old, avoid), let (mutable, block-scoped), and const (immutable reference, block-scoped). Use const by default; use let only when you need to reassign.
⚠️ typeof null === 'object' is a 27-year-old JavaScript bug that can never be fixed without breaking the web. Check for null explicitly: value === null.

exercises.question: Which keyword should you use when a variable's value will never need to change?
exercises.explanation: const is the default choice — it prevents accidental reassignment and signals intent to other developers. Use let only when you need to reassign (loop counters, accumulating values, etc.).

sections.content: ⚠️ Always use === (strict equality) not == (loose equality). == does type coercion: '0' == false is true, null == undefined is true — both dangerous bugs.

exercises.question: What is the result of: '5' === 5 in JavaScript?
exercises.explanation: '5' === 5 is false because strict equality checks both value and type. '5' is a string and 5 is a number — different types, so false. Use == if you want true (but don't).

exercises.question: Which loop is best for iterating over the values in an array?
hints: for...in is for objects; for...of is for iterables
exercises.explanation: for...of iterates over values of any iterable (arrays, strings, Sets, Maps). for...in iterates over object keys — using it on arrays gives you index strings ('0','1','2'), not values.

sections.content: 🎯 Prefer map/filter/reduce over for loops for transforming arrays. They express intent more clearly and never mutate the original.

exercises.question: Which array method returns a NEW array containing only items that pass a test function?
exercises.explanation: filter() returns a new array with only the elements where the callback returns true. map() transforms all elements. find() returns the first matching element. reduce() accumulates a single value.

exercises.question: Which syntax correctly destructures name and age from const person = { name: 'Alice', age: 25, job: 'Dev' }?
hints: Square brackets for arrays, curly braces for objects
exercises.explanation: Object destructuring uses curly braces { } and matches variable names to property keys. Array destructuring uses square brackets [ ] and matches by position.

capstoneProject.title: Data Analysis Script
capstoneProject.description: Write a JavaScript program that processes a dataset of student objects using arrays, objects, and all core concepts from this module.
requirements: An array of 10 student objects with id, name, grade, scores[] properties
Calculate average score for each student using reduce()
Filter students with average >= 80 using filter()
Map to a summary format: { name, average, passed } with map()
Find the highest achiever using reduce() or sort()
Use template literals for all console.log output
